b: Things that work well, and things that kind of failed.

I’ve been part of a growing 30+ strong design team for 6 years — a great team with a wide skill set, within a large organization. When AI became popular, Figma Make was the natural thing to try, as it lived within Figma, with a few specks of usage in Gemini and assisted user interviews (Maze), resulting in tiny glimpses of impact. Things changed quite a lot in January, as I’ve decided to take on a new challenge in a B2B e-comm scale-up as a solo UXer.

Suddenly, I faced a wall of work: support features in flight, drive discovery work, improve processes, user research, prototype, set up guidelines…the amount of split focus was scary in the beginning. I did however, see that design had the opportunity to contribute with clarity; to drive a future experience that solves user problems in a more focused way. For that to happen, though, I needed to be able to focus myself. All of this combined with the intriguing launch of Claude Code to Figma, reignited my curiosity about AI.
This works well, dangerously well | Using it almost daily.

To say that anything killed Figma is kind of lazy and silly. It’s not that I care too much about Figma, it’s more about the creative freedom to move an element from A to B in any way I want, directly on a canvas, with no intermediary interaction. Why would I give up drawing digitally with superpowers, or force myself to learn any other tool for this? However, I do think tools like Figma provided underwhelming prototyping capabilities, for far too long. Specialised software came in e.g. Axure, Protopie and excelled within their niche, but led to multi-tool management, had their own constraints and still felt slow at times. This is where AI filled in a gap, for me, especially useful being on my own.

As much as I enjoyed Figma’s variables, conditions, new actions, or a bit more overlay flexibility, it’s starting to feel like these are all mostly just constraints, considering one can go ahead and prototype much more complex interactions and flows now.

I’ve only built maybe one or two Figma click through prototypes since February. Prototyping with Claude Code enables me to express rich, complex interactions, much much faster. Practically, I often sketch ideas and tons of alternatives on paper, then materialise some of those layouts in Figma, fleshing out multiple states too. For longer, more complex journeys, I rely on FigJam diagrams too. Then I bring it all to life in Claude Code with prompts, focusing on interactions, motion and flows, resulting in a local working prototype, usually as a single .html file. It’s not always in this order, sometimes I skip steps, but it’s always a loop. The .html file is then published online, in a private prototype hub using Figma Make. The truth is always in the live web version. Technically, I can get from one end to another in only a few minutes…which allows me to iterate a lot, in many directions. The number of big or small loops until I get to a good design though… no idea, I always lose count. (Since I’ve started writing this Claude Code just released Artifacts, which I’ll test as a way to publish prototypes).

Overall, it’s been easier for me, devs, PMs, users, pretty much everyone involved in the process of building something, to interact and feel flows instead of imagining how static Figma frames move. Interpretation of how flows connect and behave often led to divergent implementation in the past, so this helped with consistency as well. What I miss in prototyping with AI is tracking relevant variety, as I explore and test. This can happen across an entire flow, on a page layout, or within a tiny component. I need something that enables me to save variation on any level, based on context and hypothesis. To deal with this, I often hide little settings panels to switch variations, but now I’m exploring a lab-like setup to visualise prototype variety on a flow and element level.
Example of a page and the set up panel I usually hide in corner pixels. Allows for switching and comparing variation on the spot.

There’s a downside to speed, though. In the beginning, I had the tendency to either jump into AI too quickly, or prompt a few too many times focusing on unnecessary details within a single direction, just because I could. Rookie mistake; associating a polished interaction and flow with a good experience. That’s something I noticed happening among the team too, with devs, PMs, others using AI to prototype, but we’ve started keeping each other accountable by going back to goals, research, testing, stepping away from the tool. Overall, given the right control and focus, this is a part of AI that helps me tremendously to build a better product and gives me back extra time to either collect feedback earlier and iterate, or explore alternatives instead of spending it on tooling.
This works well | Using it a lot

A critical point of usability testing is to give people a scenario and a clear task to be completed, then step away and shut up; let them voice their thoughts and observe what they do. The more you interrupt with “sorry, this doesn’t work; it’s just a prototype…oh…that doesn’t work either”, the less likely you are to capture a full end-to-end experience. For me, turning concepts into fully working prototypes enabled exactly this: back up and observe. Being a B2B back-end ecommerce tool, UIs and flows can get quite complex, especially when tables are at the core. Having the possibility to express a lot of depth lets participants try different pathways to achieve their goal, which in turn enabled me and the team to learn more about their mental models. There are still dead ends and not all states are covered, but prototyping with AI has given me the chance to be intentional in this aspect too. Questions as “what did you expect to happen” are now focused on parts of the experience that I truly wish to learn about, not a consequence of tooling constraints.
Adding the Excel drag to fill took a few minutes and a couple of prompts.

Adjusting context for each session and carrying data across a flow become way easier too. We’re working with different kinds of companies selling all sorts of things, from electronics to fashion. Now, as late as 15 min before a session starts, I just tell Claude “change products in this prototype to be about electronics” and it’s done. This level of nuance and detail brings a natural feeling into the research session. When it comes to carrying data over, since flows are complex, it’s important to reflect real values, sometimes created by the user, e.g., setting a product’s price, selecting a certain number of products to publish, etc. When these values don’t match across the flow, it tends to distract some participants, once again interrupting their experience.
One prompt, 35 seconds of loading time and a refresh, for all the content to change from clothing to electronics. Kept it generic for the sake of the example.
This works well | Using it biweekly

I had the chance to study different ways of coding user research, mostly within academia; it was pure research done without chasing economic impact for a product; quite refreshing to do once in a while. In a nutshell, coding is analyzing your research by going back through documentation such as recordings, notes, diaries, etc., and highlighting findings to eventually extract common themes. Handling all this data requires a lot of mental effort, but leads to a deep connection and understanding of users, while reflecting on the quality of your own method. However, realistically, I can’t spend a week analyzing interviews or testing sessions, creating video clips, documenting, and presenting it all as well…as much as I love doing this detective kind of work.
Image from Dovetail, a very useful tool for this kind of activity. Source: NNG’s article on thematic analysis and coding research https://www.nngroup.com/articles/thematic-analysis/

Therefore, I’ve been experimenting with different degrees of AI usage when synthesizing data and I’ve noticed something. Let’s say I conduct a series of 8 user interviews and discover a bunch of problems with a feature across all sessions. Since everything is recorded in Google Meet, I then ask Gemini to merge all sessions and extract common themes, quotes, and action points. This is lightning fast. However, a couple of weeks in, I recall very few of these findings, having to constantly go back to double-check what they meant. On top of that, a lot of nuance is getting lost in AI’s own interpretation and writing style. It all becomes a bit too generic or even worse, insights get skewed with words and expressions participants never used(often even when guided not to do this). The less I handle the insights myself, the less they get embedded into my design mind. I feel less confident in early design decisions, diminishing my ability to advocate for them among stakeholders.

It would be foolish to just ignore the huge advantage of speed. Currently, I use Gemini to summarise individual interviews, but also write down timestamps during the session to know which parts to rewatch, turn into clips to be shared with the team, and extract genuine quotes. Having another person join to take notes and observe helps too. I then take all the summaries and run them through AI just like before, but don’t use the outcome directly. I treat AI as a super text editor, mostly useful to validate occurrences of words and expressions, within large amounts of input. Now, I rely on those key timeframes, myself and the note taker to really form common themes and capture nuance instead. Usually, a couple of weeks later, I also force myself to go through a couple of sessions to get reconnected to participants. For now this feels like a good balance of speed and quality. It gives me back time that I use to phrase and share insights, or to run more research.
This was meh.. | Tried a couple of times only

Part of improving the current experience is a refreshed interface. The product’s functionality has grown over the years, but the UI hasn’t always kept this pace, so it was time to present all that power and data more clearly. It’s an interesting exercise, trying to capture enough of the product scope to understand core user problems without being trapped in too many edge cases and constraints. My instinct said that we needed something clear, bear bones that lets the content shine, while leveraging a few playful elements used in external materials. Nevertheless, it’s the kind of activity that requires a lot of mental space; and something that I’ve never done without a design team around. Comparing perspectives born from a similar affinity of solving other people’s problems has always been a really fun part of the process for me. That’s how I hoped to use AI too; to fill in this gap, and to have a fellow (junior?) designer next to me.

I was also hoping there was a big enough pool of training data to make AI work well for these types of elements our product mostly consists of (data dashboards, graphs, complex tables, and product cards). I was mostly looking for diversity in visual expression both in interfaces and interactions in core steps of the product. I’ve never expected end-to-end flows and perfectly tweaked screens to just pick up. Practically, I’ve tried Figma Make, Claude Code in Figma, Claude Design, and Google Stitch and I’ve been feeding them different kinds of contexts, data and prompts to get diversity in outcome.
Interestin bits and pieces that I collected across the outputs. Most of the branding and logo usage is off, but that’s less important.

The interesting takes, mostly from Claude Design and Google Stitch were getting a bit far from the brief, but in a fun way, sparking a few thoughts. Some of these turned into ideas for functionality that might or might not lead to anything, or made me wonder about details as typography scales, spacing, and elevation. Many results simply validated directions I didn’t want to take, being impractical or way too expressive, which is valuable in a way. Sadly, nothing was solid enough to inspire me to chase an entirely new direction and AI didn’t come close to being a sparring partner; it lacked the depth I was looking for, and overall like it went literally out of the box without a real purpose; the kind of quick and dirty exploration you’d do in between meetings, or Friday afternoon, that you look back at later “hmm… what was I thinking…”

To be fair, I do think that if one spends more time to iterate on guiding the AI, perhaps feeding it a more precise combination of inputs and skills, you could probably get better results. I’m saying this as things are evolving fast, and also after seeing skills like this take one, an attempt at applying Nothing’s visual style to dashboard UIs.
This works well | In trial for adoption

User research in the B2B space is quite different from research for B2C products, where I used to have quick access to a large panel of users within tools, agencies, or by simply walking outside... Even with the help of customer facing teams, reaching specific users takes time and effort — making it challenging to plan research around sprints for multiple initiatives. What if, while I empower others to run research, we use AI as a first round of user feedback? Felt so wrong to even consider this…since I’ve been trained to do the exact opposite — spend less time behind the laptop and expose the company to our users’ emotions and stories. After talking to a few other designers, and reading about companies as Synthetic users, I’ve started experimenting.

My goal was to create a UX feedback AI based skill that we can all use, to improve our work. The skill had to be aware of our business, be knowledgeable of our UX guidelines and be aware of users’ core goals and pain points. After trying a few overly complex set ups, among which was inevitably creating my own new shiny SaaS… I ended up with a skill in our repo. There were two things I’ve tweaked the most:
getting the skill to ask the right questions upfront to force people to reflect on the problem they’re solving.
providing the user perspective without extra interpretation.
The first iteration was a shared Claude project. Later this turned into a skill in the repo.

The user perspective is already surprisingly good. It analyses the context of the prompt, then replies with how different users might react to the given solution, idea, etc. It does a good job of raising pain points and whether they are addressed across different kinds of interests people have. It’s not as good at providing specific usability feedback, besides the obvious stuff. AI reduces these user portraits to lines of text, ignoring all the other context they’ve built by using this and other software. This leads to some of the suggestions being overzealous, trying to explain every element through text and icons.

Product owners were the first to try out this part of the skill, to either help with setting a direction for tricky flows, or get more perspectives on a solution they’ve had in mind. In most cases, they brought the outcome of their session back to me and we continued the discussion. I was mostly surprised to see how often they also asked the skill to visualise its output, for them.
I gave it a bad UI example , and asked specifically asked for this feedback. Normally, the skill asks questions to understand the phase its user is at: review, ideation, prototyping, etc.

The skill also checks UI pattern usage against our guidelines and components. I underestimated this initially, but then noticed how front-end engineers got excited while demo-ing it. As our goal is to become much more consistent in the interface, the skill easily catches unnecessary deviations and provides recommendations pointing to relevant guidelines and elements. Front-end engineers could get immediate feedback on their work, instead of only manually checking guidelines. We didn’t try the full loop yet, as I’m tweaking the guidelines and the skill, but I think there’s something here that will lead to increased efficiency.
Ultimately, it’s not about replacing user research because it’s not as easy to get to people; we’re doing that anyway; it’s about catching critical misjudgments early on in the process.

There are quite a few people within the organisation playing around with different AIs, to become more efficient. One of these is centralising context, starting with documentation across our tooling, using Atlassian’s Rovo agents. These have been quite useful for me, as a newcomer to a very technical company, as I must prioritise impact on users’ experience.

Instead of digging through dozens of pages and boards, while throwing tons of basic questions at a team, I first ask different Rovo agents to collect context. A few prompts and some reading later, I have a basic understanding of a concept and when things get too technical, I ask them to simplify it using metaphors and analogies. In the end, this enables me to get in and out of topics much more efficiently, leaving more time to discuss what the real issues are to be solved, and what should be improved next. Lately, as these tools have been connected with other parts of the organisation, as support, we can tap into a great deal of evidence when collecting context and help steer the conversation better. I’d love to create some kind of mega shared context that eventually combines multiple data systems and our own skills or agents, working together. When someone wants to jump right into prompting solutions, or tends to have a single path to solving a problem, this shared context (tool?) would know which core issues to raise, with clear evidence, and push them to understand the problem first.
Useful overall, definitely not an extra designer, at least not yet.

It took me around 3 months to get comfortable with the shocking speed of AI, trying out new tools and new ways of working. When it comes to what’s being said nowadays about roles becoming more fluid within the design, engineering and product trio, I have mixed feelings. The best teams I’ve been in, had people who were always curious to understand how the others work, while trusting each other’s expertise. I must admit that using a shared tool does bring us a little closer. Can we really pour our expertise into these tools, so that others can genuinely step into our roles? Not sure yet. As a solo designer, AI hasn’t necessarily given me extra hands, but it has given me a lot of time back: time to test earlier, explore more alternatives, and frame problems better, together with the team.
I spent two months building an AI workflow for my design team. Here’s what I actually learned.
AI design isn’t ugly. It’s fluent — and that’s the problem.
